column3: Pairs divine freedom from need with mercy and the power to remove a people without immediate seizure.
The immediate continuation gives destroyed towns a fixed appointment for their ruin, directly extending deferred accountability.
The closing names of forgiveness and mercy occur in a legal context and add little after the earlier closer parallel.
A named term prevents punishment from arriving at once, closely matching the focus's delay before an unavoidable event.
The nearby scene of final presentation explicitly recalls the denied appointment and supplies its setting.
Repentance and seeking forgiveness identify a possible response, but the verse adds no account of the delayed punishment.
Links being held for what one earned with the absence of protector or intercessor besides God.
The nearby parable of worldly life supplies the transient setting that precedes the focus's warning and delayed reckoning.
The paired divine names parallel the opening but do not develop its temporal or judicial claim.
Connects what people earn with an assured, swift accounting, clarifying the accountability deferred in the focus.
Its contrast between worldly adornment and enduring righteous deeds frames the local passage leading to accountability.
A request for later forgiveness shows an intercessory setting, but not the focus's divine postponement of punishment.
The Merciful grants extension to the astray until they see the promised punishment or Hour.
The local gathering of every person provides the public horizon for the focus's appointment.
False gods cannot avert harm willed by the Merciful, supporting the focus's claim of no refuge apart from Him.
After sins bring destruction, no helpers are found besides God, giving a consequential parallel to the no-refuge clause.
Exhaustive recording of deeds and the Lord's refusal to wrong anyone explain accountable earning without arbitrary haste.
The command to seek forgiveness is a general response to fault, with little connection to appointed punishment.
Mercy is self-prescribed while humanity is certainly gathered for the Day, holding mercy and final judgment together.
The nearby warning against taking Iblis and his offspring as allies prepares the failure of alternatives to God.
Its brief description of a forgiving Lord in the Sabaa narrative adds no distinct element to the focus.
Calling God Forgiving and Loving adds an affective dimension to forgiveness, though it is not about delayed reckoning.
The refusal to take misleaders as support has only a limited relation to the focus's absence of refuge.
Mercy sought for right guidance in the same surah offers a distinct protective function of mercy.
No one can shelter the messenger from God and no refuge exists apart from Him, closely echoing the final clause.
The immediate failure of invoked partners and the barrier between them make the loss of alternative refuge concrete.
The appointed courses of creation and the Forgiving name do not address culpability or deferred punishment.
Neither earnings nor false allies avail before the coming Fire, joining earned consequence with failed alternatives.
The nearby vision of the Fire ends with no way to turn away from it, an exact local counterpart to no refuge.
Divine acceptance of repentance after a battle is a limited instance of forgiveness without the focus's timing.
The demand to hasten the decisive matter contrasts with the focus's declaration that its timing is not immediate.
The nearby observation of human contentiousness gives context but does not sharpen mercy, accounting, or refuge.
The divine name the Merciful alone is too general to add to the established mercy parallels.
What the wrongdoers earned is depicted as inevitably overtaking them, supplementing the focus's conditional accounting.
The local refusal of faith and forgiveness is tied to awaiting the precedent of earlier peoples or visible punishment.
God is worthy of reverence and forgiveness, connecting moral restraint with forgiveness without cancelling judgment.
The evil results of what people earned become visible and enclose them, supplying the later outcome of the focus's delay.
A prayer combining forgiveness and mercy repeats the opening names without its judicial structure.
The direct proclamation that God is Forgiving and Merciful reinforces the focus's opening characterization.
Forgiveness and mercy appear as the source of welcome, but the reward scene is not about delayed accountability.
Moses's acknowledged self-wrong and received forgiveness give a concrete instance of mercy after culpability.
God's authority to forgive and punish together supplies the balanced divine prerogative behind the focus.
The final wall separates interior mercy from exterior punishment, a spatial image of the decisive boundary at the appointment.
The call to uprightness and seeking forgiveness before woe gives a general remedial response.
Submission to the Prophet's judgment is not a close parallel to the divine appointment or lack of refuge.
Revelation as guidance and mercy is a distinct theme with little bearing on deferred punishment.
Its inability to find transport is unrelated to the focus's refuge from divine consequence.
Creation attributed to the Merciful does not clarify the focus's mercy, accounting, or appointment.
Even intense desire for a long life cannot distance a person from punishment, qualifying the apparent length of delay.
The first human confession holds self-wronging, forgiveness, mercy, and loss together as a direct remedial counterpart.
The Lord's generosity alone does not add to the focus's account of mercy and judgment.
Believers' experience of the Kind and Merciful offers a general confirmation but no new mechanism.
The command to magnify the Lord is not materially related to the focus.
The appointed Day's ordered assembly and restricted speech sharpen the solemnity of the promised appointment.
Mercy in care for parents is a different ethical register from divine deferred accountability.
Repentance, reform, and clarification identify conditions for divine turning toward wrongdoers.
The idolaters' appeal to divine will is a context-specific excuse, only indirectly related to culpability.
People seek to hasten harm, while forgiveness is urged so that mercy may follow, closely resonating with the focus's contrast.
God's self-prescribed mercy is joined to repentance and reform after ignorant wrongdoing, specifying a route beyond culpability.
Mercy as life-giving rain does not advance the focus's moral or eschatological claim.
The paired names occur in a defense of revelation but add little to the established mercy-and-forgiveness pattern.
Those who commit evils and then repent and believe meet a Forgiving, Merciful Lord, giving a clear post-wrongdoing response.
Calamities continue until God's promise arrives, and that promise does not fail, directly supporting a fixed future fulfillment.
Entry into mercy for charitable believers is a reward theme rather than deferred accounting for wrongdoers.
Revelation is mercy, while turning from its signs brings evil punishment, giving guidance and consequence together.
The mission as mercy to all worlds is too broad to clarify the focus's delayed seizure.
God does not fail His promise to messengers; the assurance of eventual vengeance supports the appointment's certainty.
Severe punishment and forgiveness with mercy are explicitly held together, matching the focus's non-exclusive balance.
Disobedience and worldly desire are followed by pardon, showing mercy operating amid real consequences.
Mercy as removal from darkness to light is a different benefit from the focus's postponement of punishment.
The title Lord of the glorious throne has no specific bearing on the focus.
Mercy in sending a warning adds a remote connection through warning before judgment.
The youths' refusal to invoke another god is locally relevant but does not develop the focus's account of refuge or delay.
Divine victory and mercy do not clarify the focus's themes.
Moses's forty-night appointment is not an appointment of deferred accountability.
Mercy is set alongside a fulfilled word concerning Hell, preserving the tension between exception and fixed judgment.
The challenge to prove other gods has only a broad relation to the failure of alternatives.
Disbelief in the Merciful and return to the one Lord are related but add little after stronger no-alternative texts.
The challenge to false creators identifies error in idolatry but not the focus's merciful delay or appointment.
The formula naming the Merciful and Compassionate is now redundant.
False expectations and evil suspicion leading to ruin illuminate the inward posture that can precede the promised consequence.
Scripture given after earlier destructions as guidance and mercy offers only an indirect historical parallel.
The dispute over following an expedition and its gains is unrelated to the focus.
Divine bounty and mercy avert an unstated consequence, but the mechanism is not developed here.
Israel's refusal to enter the land does not clarify the focus's mercy, account, or refuge.
Rejecting God's signs and meeting entails despair of mercy and painful punishment, showing the terminal alternative.
The phrase possessor of strength is only a lexical coincidence with the focus's possessor of mercy.
Mercy expressed through beasts carrying burdens is unrelated to accountability or postponement.
An enduring punishment to the Day of Resurrection is paired with God's forgiveness and mercy, closely mirroring deferred yet real consequence.
Forgiveness and generous provision reward faithful good works, but the focus concerns wrongdoers and postponed punishment.
Finding textual inconsistency is unrelated to the focus's themes.
The pairing of might and mercy is a general divine attribute formula with little marginal contribution.
David recognizes a wrong and seeks forgiveness, but the narrative does not address the focus's delay or appointed end.
Forgiveness following a commanded humble entry is a specific ritual-historical instance with limited added value.
Pardon for the excused is a general forgiveness case without the focus's temporal or judicial structure.
Mercy and compassion avert an unstated result, largely repeating the earlier partial parallel.
Following inherited practice instead of guidance does not materially illuminate the focus.
God's call to forgiveness and Paradise appears in a marital ruling and adds little to the focus.
The mention of wombs is unrelated to mercy as the focus uses it.
Listening attentively to the Quran in hope of mercy gives a distant receptive response to divine mercy.
The preceding mission of warning and good news frames the warnings that people mock before the focus states their appointment.
The immediately preceding condemnation joins turning from reminders with forgetting what one's hands have sent ahead, directly preparing the focus's earned-accountability clause.
Respite for disbelievers is not for their good but allows sin to increase before humiliating punishment, defining the danger of delay.
Those who do evil have Hell as their refuge and find no escape from it, closely paralleling the focus's no-refuge conclusion.
Vast mercy toward people is explicitly paired with punishment that cannot be turned away from the guilty.
Every community has an appointed term that cannot be delayed or advanced once it arrives.
God withholds punishment while the Prophet is among them and while they seek forgiveness, giving a concrete account of deferred punishment.
There is no refuge from God except returning to Him, making the focus's denial of any other shelter explicit.
If God hastened evil for people as they seek good, their term would already be finished; the verse directly contrasts haste and reprieve.
Each community has a term that neither comes early nor late, reinforcing the fixed appointment.
Wrongdoers cannot escape God on earth and have no protectors besides Him, combining failed flight with failed alternatives.
The Lord does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reforming, qualifying punishment with divine justice.
The Lord's forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing is set beside the severity of His punishment.
Earlier disbelievers were granted respite and then seized, supplying a historical pattern for the focus's postponed consequence.
Forgiveness is offered together with being deferred to an appointed term, closely matching both halves of the focus.
God is not unaware of wrongdoers but postpones them until a Day, making delayed judgment explicit.
No community can precede or postpone its appointed term, a concise parallel to the fixed appointment.
If God seized people for their wrongdoing, no creature would remain, but He defers them to an appointed term; this is the closest verbal and thematic parallel.
Punishment is withheld until a messenger has been sent, adding a stated condition to divine restraint.
The command not to hasten against them, while their days are being counted, depicts measured rather than immediate reckoning.
A prior decree and an appointed term prevent an immediate, inevitable punishment.
The Lord does not destroy towns until He raises a messenger among them, further specifying restraint before punishment.
A brief enjoyment is followed by compulsion to severe punishment, giving a limited temporal parallel.
A nearer punishment precedes the greater one so that people may return, suggesting judgment can be graduated rather than immediate.
If God seized people for what they earned, no creature would remain, but He postpones them to an appointed term; it is an especially exact parallel.
Continued enjoyment until a time is expressly described as mercy, connecting mercy with temporal reprieve.
God's expansive mercy and forgiveness address those who have wronged themselves, supplying the redemptive side of culpability.
People are commanded to turn back before punishment comes suddenly, after which they cannot be helped.
God is Forgiver of sin and Accepter of repentance while also severe in punishment, preserving the focus's paired attributes.
Misfortune comes through what hands have earned, yet God pardons much, directly pairing earned consequence with forbearance.
God can destroy for what people earn and yet pardons much, another direct formulation of accountable restraint.
Forgiveness toward those who do not expect God's days is set beside God's recompense of each people for what they earned.
Every soul is repaid for what it earned without wrong, clarifying the justice of the delayed account.
The Lord's vast forgiveness is stated in the context of moral failure and restraint from major sins.
If God wills destruction or mercy, none can protect the disbelievers from painful punishment.
God forgives sins and defers people to an appointed term, directly uniting forgiveness with a fixed delay.
